docs.title: Welcome to the EMBER Archive Documentation
What is EMBER?
docs.text:
EMBER is the Ecosystem for Multimodal Brain-behavior Experimentation and Research.

The EMBER Archive enables storage, sharing, and analysis of multimodal neurophysiological and behavioral data, primarily supporting the Brain Behavior Quantification and Synchronization (BBQS) Program.

As you deposit data, the most important thing is to determine if your data contains sensitive human data that should not be shared with the public. If you have sensitive data you should upload such data to EMBER-Vault (coming soon!). Other data may go to EMBER-DANDI, where standard embargo options are available. It is your job as PI to consult with your IRB and other relevant entities to ensure that data can be shared.

Regardless of what resource you choose, the main goal is to deposit data such that a secondary user can reuse data for analyses. To accomplish this, you will need to convert your data with existing standards (NWB/BIDS). This document will also help you think through how to use these standards to best fit your data.

If you are part of a BBQS team, you can contact us at help@emberarchive.org for additional help/resources.

docs.title: Storage Platforms
docs.text:
If your data are:

  • animal data or de-identified human data, use EMBER-DANDI, which supports multimodal data from both animals and humans. Human data must not contain any PHI/PII and must be completely deidentified.
  • sensitive human data, use EMBER-Vault, which supports HIPAA aligned, restricted human data storage

How EMBER is architected to support neuroscience

EMBER-DANDI is the open data archive that can store animal and de-identified human data. EMBER-Vault is a HIPAA-compliant storage for identifiable human data, such as raw video and audio.

docs.title: How do I use EMBER-DANDI?
docs.text:
1. Create an account for EMBER-DANDI as described in the User Guide.
  2. Standardize your data using community standards Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) and/or Neurodata without Borders (NWB).
  3. Finally, upload your standardized data to EMBER-DANDI.
  4. You can embargo your dataset for a desired period of time, which means it is viewable only to you and selected individuals.
  5. You can publish your dataset, making it publicly available and creating a DOI.

docs.title: How do I use EMBER-Vault?
docs.text:
COMING SOON

Read more about it at our EMBER-Vault page, and contact us for more details at help@emberarchive.org.

docs.title: Standardizing Data
docs.text:
Data standardization into BIDS and/or NWB is required for uploading to either of the EMBER storage platforms to enable easy and accessible reuse of data by secondary users who were not involved in the original study that created the data. We show one example of reproducing published figures using the NWB version of a BBQS dataset at Example Standardization and Reproducibility.

BIDS broadly describes how to rename files and folders and organize them into a standardized directory. It also requires associated metadata files to help explain the experiment and data.

NWB is a specific file type that can store one or more modalities within it. Relevant metadata is also stored directly inside the NWB file.

The recommended approach for standardiziation is as follows:

  • If there is a data standardization scheme that you or your field is most comfortable using, then prioritize that
  • Otherwise, we recommend that you try to get your data packaged into NWB as much as possible, and then utilize BIDS as the folder/file organization/naming scheme to capture the rest of the information
  • If you already have multimodal data that are packaged into a single-ish file, collected at the same time point, etc., then use NWB
  • If your data are already organized in a file structure corresponding to session, subject, modality, etc., then use BIDS
  • If a bit a both, consider a hybrid option

docs.title: I'm new to these standards - how can I get help?
docs.text:
More specific instructions for how to standardize data can be found in the User Guide.

If you need help, please reach out to help@emberarchive.org.

docs.text:
EMBER is also planning development a cloud-based analysis ecosystem cocnnected to the data storage resources:

  • EMBER-Hearth: enables analysis pipelines such as spike sorting and pose estimation inference in the cloud through both of these platforms.

Envisioned connection of analysis platform EMBER-Hearth to EMBER's data storage platforms.

docs.title: Example Workflow for Data Standardization and Analysis Reproducibility
docs.text:
Here we document an example of how we

  1. standardized data into a community-accepted standard (NWB) and
  2. enabled reproducibility of paper figures as a starting point for secondary analyses.

In doing this exercise, we complete a pipeline that is key for any datasets that are uploaded to EMBER. It is important that not only is the data standardized for improved storage and metadata retrieval, but that the standardized data can also be used for secondary processing and analyses. Reproducing key figures is the first such verification step towards ensuring that open datasets can be repurposed for new scientific endeavours.

docs.title: Public Products
docs.text:
1. Conversion script from the original processed data files to a single NWB
  2. Jupyter notebook to recreate paper figures from the NWB file

docs.title: Original dataset
docs.text: The original dataset is associated with the paper Human neural dynamics of real-world and imagined navigation, authored by a BBQS Team (Dr. Nanthia Suthana, PI). It contains four .mat files containing highly processed data for each of the four figures of the paper. In addition, the MATLAB codes to generate each figure are comprised of four .m files.

docs.title: Conversion
docs.text:
In collaboration with Dr. Suthana and Dr. Seeber (lead author), we explored each of the data variables in the original .mat files and identified analogous containers within the NWB file structure.

Most of the data variables are relevant to multiple subjects at the same time (e.g., group averages).

Because of this, we opted to convert the data into an NWB extension: ndx-multisubjects. In addition to group averages, this extension is also suitable for storing sensor data that encompasses multiple subjects at once (e.g., video of multiple subjects in an environment, microphone data capturing audio from multiple sources, etc).

Each variable within the .mat files was then converted into the appropriate modality type within NWB with the relevant metadata capture (sampling rates, start times, descriptions of variables).

Each variable of the four .mat files was converted into a container within a single NWB file

The current version of the conversion script is located at https://github.com/brain-bbqs/reproforce/blob/main/suthana/Suthana_Zenodo_Conversion.py.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
To verify that the original data was properly converted into NWB, we checked whether the NWB data could be used to replicate the MATLAB code and resulting figures.

We were able to recreate all figures from the original paper.

The current notebook for recreating figures is located at https://github.com/brain-bbqs/reproforce/blob/main/suthana/create_figs_Zenodo.ipynb.

Below are a few examples:

Fig. 1 Original

Fig. 1d recreated in Python with NWB data

Fig 2. Original

Fig. 2b top recreated in Python with NWB data Fig. 3 Original

Fig. 3a recreated in Python with NWB data Fig. 4 Original

Fig. 4g recreated in Python with NWB data

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
As mentioned above, the first step towards enabling robust secondary analyses is to replicate publication figures or analyses produced with the original file format.

To continue towards this effort, the following next steps are outlined to enable novel analyses that are best served with the richness of raw data.

  • once final reviews of the converted Zenodo data are complete, upload the NWB file as a version 2 of the Zenodo dataset (with permissions from Dr. Seeber and Dr. Suthana)
  • convert original raw data into NWB
  • replicate analyses from the original raw data stored in NWB, using the processed Zenodo data as an intermediate check
  • perform secondary (new) analyses

docs.title: What is EMBER?
docs.text:
EMBER is the Ecosystem for Multi-Modal Brain-behavior Experimentation and Research.

The EMBER Archive enables storage, sharing, and analysis of multimodal neurophysiological and behavioral data, primarily supporting the Brain Behavior Quantification and Synchronization (BBQS) Program.

docs.title: Storage and Analytics Platforms
docs.text:
EMBER has two data storage platforms:

  • EMBER-DANDI: supports multimodal data from both animals and humans. Human data must not contain any PHI/PII and must be completely deidentified.
  • EMBER-Vault: supports HIPAA aligned, restricted human data storage

EMBER is also planning development a cloud-based analysis ecosystem cocnnected to the data storage resources:

  • EMBER-Hearth: enables analysis pipelines such as spike sorting and pose estimation inference in the cloud through both of these platforms.

(A) EMBER architecture

(B) EMBER-DANDI and EMBER-Vault

EMBER-DANDI is the open data archive that can store animal and de-identified human data. EMBER-Vault is a HIPAA-compliant storage for identifiable human data, such as raw video and audio.

docs.title: How do I upload data?
docs.text:
1. Create an account for each appropriate storage platform using instructions in the User Guide.
  2. Standardize your data using community standards Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) and/or Neurodata without Borders (NWB).
  3. Upload the standardized data to the appropriate storage platform(s) using instructions in the User Guide.

docs.title: Standardizing Data
docs.text:
Data standardization is required for uploading to either of the EMBER storage platforms to enable easy and accessible reuse of data by secondary users who were not involved in the original study that created the data.

The recommended approach is to organize your dataset using the BIDS schema and convert relevant file contents per session into NWB.

BIDS broadly describes how to rename files and folders and organize them into a standardized directory. It also requires associated metadata files to help explain the experiment and data.

NWB is a specific file type that can store one or more modalities within per experimental session. Relevant metadata is also stored directly inside the NWB file.

Here is a minimal multimodal dataset layout as an example, including iEEG in NWB formats and audio and video files:

my_dataset/
├── dataset_description.json
├── participants.tsv
├── participants.json
├── sub-01/
│   ├── ses-01/
│   │   ├── ieeg/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.nwb
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.json
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_channels.tsv
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_electrodes.tsv
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_events.tsv
│   │   │
│   │   ├── beh/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_beh.tsv
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_beh.json
│   │   │
│   │   ├── video/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_video.mp4
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_video.json
│   │   │
│   │   └── audio/
│   │       ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_audio.wav
│   │       └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_audio.json

docs.title: I'm new to these standards - how can I get help?
docs.text:
More specific instructions for how to standardize data can be found in the User Guide.

You are welcome to consult external sources (websites, LLMs, coding harnesses) to help you standardize your data, but please ensure that converted data has been checked for quality.

If you are using an AI-based or -assisted workflow, please make sure to exercise due diligence to check for quality/accuracy, understanding that it is ultimately the Principal Investigator's responsibility to make the data truly reusable by other investigators.

If you need help, please reach out to help@emberarchive.org.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
1. The first step is to standardize your data, which will be similar regardless of whether you are using EMBER-DANDI or EMBER-Vault.

  2. After standardizing the data, you must validate the converted data using the DANDI CLI.

  3. Create account(s) for the appropriate storage platform(s).

  4. Finally, upload your validated and standardized data to the appropriate storage platform EMBER-DANDI or EMBER-Vault.

docs.title: EMBER-DANDI: Account Setup
docs.text: EMBER-DANDI is the subsystem of the EMBER archive designed to store de-identified, non-PHI/PII data, which can include both animal and human data. It is suitable for human neural and behavioral experiments with non-sensitive data. EMBER-DANDI data is intended to eventually be open to the public, but does support embargoed datasets which would remain private for a set period of time (i.e., after results have been published).

docs.title: GitHub Account Setup
docs.text:
1. Create a GitHub Account
    • If not already a GitHub user, sign up here.
  2. Register on EMBER
    • Navigate to the EMBER-DANDI portal and click the Login button in the top right corner.
  3. Account Review and Approval
    • After registering, you will receive an email confirming that your account is under review.
    • While we try to review and approve accounts as soon as possible, this is a manual process and some reviews may take an extended time, especially for new GitHub accounts or non .edu email addresses.
  4. Access EMBER
    • Upon approval, you will be able to access EMBER by logging in through the Login button in the top right corner.

docs.title: Getting Started with the DANDI Client
docs.text: In these instructions, you will install Python 3.9+ and then install the DANDI Python Client.

docs.title: Install Python
docs.text:
If you're new to Python, it may be useful to start by checking out Python's Getting Started page There are many ways to install and use Python, so we've highlighted a few common ways to get started below.

  • Install Anaconda
  • Install uv

docs.title: Install the DANDI Client
docs.text:
Once you've gotten up and running with Python, the following command will install the DANDI Client: 

pip install -U dandi

docs.text:
For more detailed information on the DANDI Python Client, please refer to the following resources:

docs.title: Data Standardization for EMBER-DANDI and EMBER-Vault
docs.text:
This guide walks you through a suggested procedure on how to prepare your dataset for upload using the BIDS standard, with support for intracranial recordings, audio/video, and behavioral data, and optional use of NWB files.

This covers:

  1. The relevant standards
  2. The standardization process and examples
  3. BIDS Standard
  4. Human Audio/Video
  5. Validation
  6. Common Pitfalls
  7. Recommended Workflow

docs.title: 1. Relevant Data Standards
docs.text:
Before formatting your dataset, familiarize yourself with the standards supported by the BBQS Program and the EMBER archive (defined by the BBQS DCAIC Data Standards Working Group):

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vIJ01La9G76FfGywS3IbG4o1GR4qquS31MoJ2B4_4os/edit?usp=sharing

A quick summary relevant to sensitive, multimodal human datasets (such as audio/video of participants) is outlined below.

docs.title: Core BIDS
docs.text:
• BIDS specification: https://bids.neuroimaging.io/
  • Defines folder structure, file naming, file types and metadata conventions for different data types

docs.title: Intracranial / Microelectrode Data
docs.text: https://bids-specification.readthedocs.io/en/stable/modality-specific-files/intracranial-electroencephalography.html

docs.title: MEG Data
docs.text: https://bids-specification.readthedocs.io/en/stable/modality-specific-files/magnetoencephalography.html#meg-recording-data

docs.title: BEP032 (microelectrode extensions)
docs.text:
https://bids.neuroimaging.io/extensions/beps/bep_032.html

Use for:

  • Depth electrodes
  • Microelectrode arrays
  • Spike/LFP recordings

docs.title: BEP047 (motion, audio, video)
docs.text:
https://bids.neuroimaging.io/extensions/beps/bep_047.html

Use for:

  • Video recordings (e.g., behavior, eye tracking)
  • Audio recordings (speech, environment)
  • Motion capture

docs.title: NWB (Neurodata Without Borders)
docs.text:
https://www.nwb.org/

Recommended for:

  • Spike times
  • LFP
  • Rich electrophysiology metadata

Important

If using NWB files, we recommend the files should still be organized within a BIDS structure.

NWB extensions can be found at https://nwb-extensions.github.io

For multi-subject data (multiple subjects interacting, recorded at the same time), refer to ndx-multisubjects

ndx-multisubjects

This extension is undergoing development, and currently will not pass the validator. You can still use and upload this file to EMBER-DANDI using --validation skip argument until the validators are updated or this extension is incorporated into core NWB.

docs.title: 2. Standardization Workflow
docs.text: Preparing your dataset involves three main steps:

docs.title: Step 1: Organize Files into BIDS Structure
docs.text:
• Create folders and filenames according to BIDS rules
  • Convert to allowable filetypes if needed

docs.title: Step 2: Add Metadata
docs.text:
• JSON sidecars
  • TSV files (events, channels, electrodes, etc.)
  • Advise to use LinkML to create/describe their metadata. For advanced: point to complete systems like from Juelich
  • Advise to use established lab notebook systems to formalize

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Locally
docs.text:
• Use the dandi-cli (which used the NWB inspector, BIDS Validator (https://bids.neuroimaging.io/tools/validator.html) etc) before uploading.
  • Please see the instructions here: https://github.com/dandi/dandi-cli

docs.title: 1. Folder Structure (Core BIDS Template)
docs.text:
BIDS specifies a particular set of folders and file names to organize data:

https://bids.neuroimaging.io/getting_started/folders_and_files/index.html

More examples will be made available at:

https://github.com/brain-bbqs

Here is a minimal multimodal dataset layout as an example, including iEEG in NWB formats and audio and video files:

my_dataset/
├── dataset_description.json
├── participants.tsv
├── participants.json
├── sub-01/
│   ├── ses-01/
│   │   ├── ieeg/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.nwb
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.json
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_channels.tsv
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_electrodes.tsv
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_events.tsv
│   │   │
│   │   ├── beh/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_beh.tsv
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_beh.json
│   │   │
│   │   ├── video/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_video.mp4
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_video.json
│   │   │
│   │   └── audio/
│   │       ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_audio.wav
│   │       └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_audio.json

docs.title: 2. BIDS File Naming Rules
docs.text:
As you go, please be sure to refer to the BIDS examples: https://github.com/bids-standard/bids-examples

BIDS uses structured filenames:

sub-<participant>[_ses-<session>]_task-<task>[_modality]

Examples:

  • sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.nwb
  • sub-01_ses-01_task-speaking_audio.wav
  • sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_video.mp4

docs.title: 3.1 dataset_description.json
docs.text:
{
  "Name": "Example Multimodal Dataset",
  "BIDSVersion": "1.9.0",
  "DatasetType": "raw",
  "Authors": ["Jane Doe", "John Smith"]
}

docs.title: 3.2 participants.tsv
docs.text:
participant_id  age sex
sub-01  29  M
sub-02  34  F

docs.title: channels.tsv
docs.text:
name    type    units   sampling_frequency
chan01  microelectrode  uV  30000

docs.title: electrodes.tsv
docs.text:
name    x   y   z
elec01  12.3    -45.2   30.1

docs.title: 3.4 events.tsv
docs.text:
onset   duration    trial_type
0.0 1.0 stimulus
2.0 1.5 response

docs.title: 3.5 Sidecar JSON Example
docs.text:
For an iEEG file:

{
  "SamplingFrequency": 30000,
  "PowerLineFrequency": 60,
  "iEEGReference": "common average",
  "TaskName": "rest"
}

docs.title: 4. Using NWB within BIDS
docs.text: If using NWB files within your project, they can be used to represent key time series data within BIDS, such as iEEG.

docs.title: Recommended approach
docs.text:
• Store electrophysiology data as .nwb files
  • Keep behavioral, events, and metadata in BIDS sidecars
  • Organize the dataset with NWB files within the BIDS structure, getting the best of both worlds

Example:

sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.nwb
sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_events.tsv
sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.json

When combining these standards, our key recommendations are:

  • NWB = data container
  • BIDS = dataset organization + metadata standard

docs.title: 4. Human Audio / Video (BEP047)
docs.text:
Supported formats:

  • Video: mp4, avi
  • Audio: wav

Example sidecar:

{
  "SamplingFrequency": 48000,
  "Microphone": "Shure SM7B"
}

For video:

{
  "FrameRate": 30,
  "Resolution": "1920x1080"
}

docs.title: 5. Validation (Required Before Upload)
docs.text: Data uploaded to either EMBERVault or EMBER-DANDI must be properly standardized.

docs.title: Command Line Validation for BIDS (Recommended)
docs.text:
You can find detailed instructions on use of the BIDS validator here:

https://bids.neuroimaging.io/tools/validator.html

We do not recommend using the online data validator for datasets containing PHI/PII.

https://bids-validator.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/command-line.html

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
(Use the Mac Terminal, Linux Command Line, or Windows Subsystem for Linux)

Using Deno:

https://docs.deno.com/runtime/getting_started/installation/

deno install -ERWN -g -n bids-validator jsr:@bids/validator

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
deno run -ERWN jsr:@bids/validator <dataset>

When using an extension, you must use the flag --schema with the link to the pull request specific to the extension.

docs.title: BEP032
docs.text: --schema https://bids-specification--2307.org.readthedocs.build/en/2307/schema.json

docs.title: BEP047
docs.text: --schema https://bids-specification--2231.org.readthedocs.build/en/2231/schema.json

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
• No errors → ready to upload
  • Warnings → usually acceptable but should be reviewed
  • Errors → must fix before upload to EMBER-Vault

Warning

If you are using NWB files at all, you will need to validate those separately using the DANDI CLI

docs.title: Incorrect filenames
docs.text: • Missing task- or sub- labels

docs.title: Missing JSON sidecars
docs.text: • Especially for iEEG and video/audio

docs.title: Inconsistent sampling rates
docs.text: • Must match metadata

docs.title: Time misalignment
docs.text:
• Ensure events align across modalities

If your team is struggling, the EMBER archive team can help. Reach out at info@emberarchive.org.

docs.title: 7. Recommended Workflow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Prepare raw data

    • Export from acquisition systems
    • Convert relevant modalities to NWB if appropriate, convert other data types to appropriate BIDS formats

  2. Create folder structure

    mkdir -p my_dataset/sub-01/ses-01/ieeg

  3. Rename files to BIDS format

  4. Create metadata files

    • dataset_description.json
    • participants.tsv
    • sidecars

  5. Add events + behavioral data

  6. Validate BIDS dataset

  7. Fix errors

  8. Upload to platform

docs.title: Information Needed to Inform Standard(s) Used
docs.text:
The following information is used to determine best practices and what standard(s) to use for your data:

  • Modalities: types of data streams (e.g., EEG, kinematic, EMG, audio, video, annotations)
  • Metadata: critical information a secondary user would need to interpret values correctly and have sufficient context for the experiment (e.g., sampling rates, channel identity, stimulus timing, events)
  • Data Structure: format of the data (e.g., do you have data split into different sections, are they continuous with each other, how does this structure connect to the greater context of the experiment, how are different experimental sessions represented)
  • Data Tier: rawness of data you are sharing (e.g., straight off the device, featurized)

There can also be many nuances within the data that should be captured:

  • Uniquely formatted data: example: spreadsheets of detailed notes relating to certain experiment sessions
  • Exceptions: some recording sessions were not good, some channels were bad, some modalities were not recorded for a particular session
  • Long chronic data: does it make sense to split up the chronic data by hour, day, weeks?

Many of these above nuances can impact the logistical details of how data is packaged into a standard. The standardization plan and packaging strategy suited for your data may be informed by how you actually analyze the original data. If your analysis script uses data that has been curated into a single .mat file or .h5 for instance, NWB could be a natural reflection of that. In contrast, if your analysis script pulls in data stored in modality-separated folders, BIDS may fit better.

You can see an example of reproducing analysis (figures) at Example Standardization and Reproducibility using data that was originally in .mat files and converted into NWB.

Relevant Standards

Before formatting your dataset, familiarize yourself with the standards supported by the BBQS Program and the EMBER archive (defined by the BBQS DCAIC Data Standards Working Group) using the BBQS standardization document.

A quick summary relevant to common data modalities is outlined below:

BIDS: Brain Imaging Data Structure
  • BIDS specification: Defines folder structure, file naming, file types and metadata conventions for different data types
  • BIDS extensions:
    • iEEG/EEG
    • MEG Data
    • BEP 032 (microelectrode extension), used for depth electrodes, microelectrode arrays, and spike/LFP recordings
    • BEP 047 (motion, audio, video), used for video recordings (e.g., behavior, eye tracking), audio recordings (speech, environment), and motion capture
NWB: Neurodata Without Borders
  • NWB specification, well-suited for spike times, LFP, Rich electrophysiology metadata,general time series, all-in-one file approach, compatible with several analysis and visualization tools.
  • NWB in Python (pynwb)
  • NWB in MATLAB (matnwb)
  • NWB extensions:
    • pose estimation (ndx-pose)
    • multiple subjects interacting together (ndx-multisubjects)
    • audio (ndx-sound)
  • streamlined converters in Python (neuroconv)

Important

If using NWB files, we recommend the files should still be organized within a BIDS structure.

docs.title: Data Standardization Recommendation for Animal Data and De-identified Human Data: EMBER-DANDI
Animal Data
docs.text: COMING SOON

docs.title: Example 1 - Audio, Video, and pose estimation (SLEAP) in NWB
docs.text:
Let's suppose the original data is a single animal in cage with one camera and two microphones:

myExperimentSession/

Each of the audio and video files in the folder1 in myExperiment hold data that is continuous in time with the files of folder2, which is continuous with folder3 and so and and so forth. Altogether, folders 1 - 5 constitute a single recording session. This means that all the data should be contained inside a single NWB file.

To make it easier for a secondary user to parse the data, then, we will concatenate all video files together, all audio files together, and all pose data together within the single NWB file.

The resulting NWB structure then looks like:

docs.title: Example 2 - Audio and Video in BIDS, and pose estimation (SLEAP) in NWB
docs.text:
Now let's suppose we want to instead use BIDS, which would allow us to maintain the original way we had split up the experiment session. We can also keep the original data formats for audio and video files.

The BIDS layout would look like: 

dataset/
    sub-01/
        ses-01/
            beh/
               audio-part1.wav
               video-part1.mp4

docs.title: De-identified Human Data
docs.text: COMING SOON

docs.title: Example 1 - iEEG and motion in NWB
Example 2 - iEEG and motion in hybrid BIDS/NWB
Data Standardization Recommendation for PHI/PII Human Data: EMBER-Vault
docs.text:
This guide walks you through a suggested procedure on how to prepare your dataset for upload using the BIDS standard, with support for common data types such as intracranial recordings, audio/video, and behavioral data, and optional use of NWB files.

This covers:

  1. The standardization process and examples
  2. BIDS Standard
  3. Audio/Video
  4. Validation
  5. Common Pitfalls
  6. Recommended Workflow

docs.title: 1. Standardization Workflow
docs.text: Preparing your dataset involves three main steps:

docs.title: Step 1: Organize Files into BIDS Structure
docs.text:
• Create folders and filenames according to BIDS rules
  • Convert to allowable filetypes if needed

docs.title: Step 2: Add Metadata
docs.text:
• JSON sidecars
  • TSV files (events, channels, electrodes, etc.)
  • Advise to use LinkML to create/describe their metadata. For advanced: point to complete systems like from Juelich
  • Advise to use established lab notebook systems to formalize

docs.title: Step 3: Validate Locally
docs.text:
• Use the dandi-cli (which used the NWB inspector, BIDS Validator (https://bids.neuroimaging.io/tools/validator.html) etc) before uploading.
  • Please see the instructions here: https://github.com/dandi/dandi-cli

docs.title: 3.1. Folder Structure (Core BIDS Template)
docs.text:
BIDS specifies a particular set of folders and file names to organize data:

https://bids.neuroimaging.io/getting_started/folders_and_files/index.html

More examples will be made available at:

https://github.com/brain-bbqs

Here is a minimal multimodal dataset layout as an example, including iEEG in NWB formats and audio and video files:

my_dataset/
├── dataset_description.json
├── participants.tsv
├── participants.json
├── sub-01/
│   ├── ses-01/
│   │   ├── ieeg/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.nwb
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.json
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_channels.tsv
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_electrodes.tsv
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_events.tsv
│   │   │
│   │   ├── beh/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_beh.tsv
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_beh.json
│   │   │
│   │   ├── video/
│   │   │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_video.mp4
│   │   │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_video.json
│   │   │
│   │   └── audio/
│   │       ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_audio.wav
│   │       └── sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_audio.json

docs.title: 3.2. BIDS File Naming Rules
docs.text:
As you go, please be sure to refer to the BIDS examples: https://github.com/bids-standard/bids-examples

BIDS uses structured filenames:

sub-<participant>[_ses-<session>]_task-<task>[_modality]

Examples:

  • sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.nwb
  • sub-01_ses-01_task-speaking_audio.wav
  • sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_video.mp4

docs.title: 3.3.1 dataset_description.json
docs.text:
{
  "Name": "Example Multimodal Dataset",
  "BIDSVersion": "1.9.0",
  "DatasetType": "raw",
  "Authors": ["Jane Doe", "John Smith"]
}

docs.title: 3.3.2 participants.tsv
docs.text:
participant_id  age sex
sub-01  29  M
sub-02  34  F

docs.title: channels.tsv
docs.text:
name    type    units   sampling_frequency
chan01  microelectrode  uV  30000

docs.title: electrodes.tsv
docs.text:
name    x   y   z
elec01  12.3    -45.2   30.1

docs.title: 3.3.4 events.tsv
docs.text:
onset   duration    trial_type
0.0 1.0 stimulus
2.0 1.5 response

docs.title: 3.3.5 Sidecar JSON Example
docs.text:
For an iEEG file:

{
  "SamplingFrequency": 30000,
  "PowerLineFrequency": 60,
  "iEEGReference": "common average",
  "TaskName": "rest"
}

docs.title: 3.4. Using NWB within BIDS
docs.text: If using NWB files within your project, they can be used to represent key time series data within BIDS, such as iEEG.

docs.title: Recommended approach
docs.text:
• Store electrophysiology data as .nwb files
  • Keep behavioral, events, and metadata in BIDS sidecars
  • Organize the dataset with NWB files within the BIDS structure, getting the best of both worlds

Example:

sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.nwb
sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_events.tsv
sub-01_ses-01_task-rest_ieeg.json

When combining these standards, our key recommendations are:

  • NWB = data container
  • BIDS = dataset organization + metadata standard

docs.title: 4. Audio / Video (BEP047)
docs.text:
Supported formats:

  • Video: mp4, avi
  • Audio: wav

Example sidecar:

{
  "AudioSampleRate": 48000,
  "ManufacturersModelName: "Shure SM7B"
}

For video:

{
  "VideoFrameRate": 30,
  "ImageWidth": "1920",
  "ImageHeight": "1080"
}

docs.title: 5. Validation (Required Before Upload)
docs.text: Data uploaded to either EMBERVault or EMBER-DANDI must be properly standardized.

docs.title: Command Line Validation for BIDS (Recommended)
docs.text:
You can find detailed instructions on use of the BIDS validator here:

https://bids.neuroimaging.io/tools/validator.html

IMPORTANT: Keep in mind that some tools such as online validators may send parts of your data outside your local system. It is the job of the Principal Investigator to ensure that all data handling, especially for sensitive human data, is in alignment with existing laws, regulations, and policy, including terms of data sharing as agreed by the human participants through the informed consent process.

https://bids-validator.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/command-line.html

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
(Use the Mac Terminal, Linux Command Line, or Windows Subsystem for Linux)

Using Deno:

https://docs.deno.com/runtime/getting_started/installation/

deno install -ERWN -g -n bids-validator jsr:@bids/validator

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
deno run -ERWN jsr:@bids/validator <dataset>

When using a BEP standard, you must use the flag --schema with the link to the pull request specific to the extension.

docs.title: BEP032
docs.text: --schema https://bids-specification--2307.org.readthedocs.build/en/2307/schema.json

docs.title: BEP047
docs.text: --schema https://bids-specification--2231.org.readthedocs.build/en/2231/schema.json

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
• No errors → ready to upload
  • Warnings → usually acceptable but should be reviewed
  • Errors → must fix before upload to EMBER-Vault

Warning

If you are using NWB files at all, you will need to validate those separately using the DANDI CLI

docs.title: Incorrect filenames
docs.text: • Missing task- or sub- labels

docs.title: Missing JSON sidecars
docs.text: • Especially for iEEG and video/audio

docs.title: Inconsistent sampling rates
docs.text: • Must match metadata

docs.title: Time misalignment
docs.text:
• Ensure events align across modalities

If your team is struggling, the EMBER archive team can help. Reach out at help@emberarchive.org.

docs.title: 7. Recommended Workflow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Prepare raw data

    • Export from acquisition systems
    • Convert relevant modalities to NWB if appropriate, convert other data types to appropriate BIDS formats

  2. Create folder structure

    mkdir -p my_dataset/sub-01/ses-01/ieeg

  3. Rename files to BIDS format

  4. Create metadata files

    • dataset_description.json
    • participants.tsv
    • sidecars

  5. Add events + behavioral data

  6. Validate BIDS dataset

  7. Fix errors

  8. Upload to platform

docs.text:
These instructions will guide you on how to download data to EMBER-DANDI.

Below, we have provided one set of instructions for users that are new to EMBER-DANDI, and one set for experienced users. Please follow whichever best fits your needs:

  1. I've used DANDI or CLI tools before
  2. I'm new to Python, CLI, and/or DANDI

docs.title: Download a full dandiset
docs.text:
The following is a quick reference for downloading data using the DANDI Client: 

dandi download https://dandi.emberarchive.org/dandiset/<dandiset_id>/<version>

docs.title: Install Python and the DANDI Client
docs.text: Please refer to our Dandi Client instructions.

docs.title: Download a full dandiset
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the dandiset of interest on EMBER-DANDI

  2. Click the "Download" tab on the right-hand panel.

    • Hint: If you want a different version of the dandiset than the default, click the dropdown labeled "Download a different version?" and select the desired version.

  3. Copy the command and paste it into your terminal. For example, 

    dandi download https://dandi.emberarchive.org/dandiset/<dandiset_id>/draft

docs.title: Download a single file
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the dandiset of interest on EMBER-DANDI

  2. Click the "Files" tab on the right-hand panel.

  3. On the file explorer page for the dandiset, navigate to the folder containing the desired file (if not at the root level)

  4. Click the download button on the desired file.

docs.title: EMBER-Vault: Account Setup
docs.text:
COMING SOON! This documentation is meant to give a sense of capabilities

EMBER-Vault is in active development and is currently undergoing beta testing with a small subset of users. If you are interested in testing EMBER-Vault in this phase or have any current needs for sensitive human data storage, please contact us at help@emberarchive.org."

EMBER-Vault is the subsystem of the EMBER archive designed to store and control access to sensitive human data, including human health data and identifiable human data. It is suitable for human neural and behavioral experiments with sensitive data, and is not appropriate for open data release or animal data. It is compliant and aligned with relevant standards for PHI/PII data storage.

For more in-depth information on the recommended data standardization workflow, see the guide on data standardization

This resource is under active development, and we anticipate EMBER-Vault will be available soon!

docs.title: Globus Account Setup
docs.text:
Pre-requisite

You will need to have an active Globus account, which can usually be obtained through your academic institution.

  1. Request access to EMBER-Vault by contacting EMBER admins. You will be asked to provide information and reasoning as to why you need an EMBER-Vault account which will be used to determine your eligibility
  2. If and when your account is approved, EMBER admins will contact you providing your EMBER-Vault username and temporary password as well as the name of your EMBER-Vault project collection
  3. Log in to Globus. This can be done through your institution's authentication method
  4. Navigate to your EMBER-Vault project collection
  5. Select File Manager
  6. Type in Collection name
  7. Select Collection
  8. Follow the steps to link your Globus and EMBER-Vault accounts.
  9. Once you have authenticated with EMBER-Vault and linked your accounts, you will be routed back to File Manager and see the following:
    1. Do not press continue
  10. Respond to your EMBER-Vault onboarding email to let EMBER admins know so they can connect your user to the data store
  11. Once you receive confirmation from EMBER admins to continue, sign back in to Globus and EMBER-Vault navigating to your EMBER-Vault project collection. You should now have full access and be able to download/upload data as your permissions allow

docs.title: Uploading Data
docs.text: COMING SOON! This documentation is meant to give a sense of capabilities.

docs.title: Data Upload
docs.text:
Once your user account and project have been set up, you are ready to upload your validated data to EMBER-Vault! To use EMBER-Vault, you must validate your dataset locally. The EMBER-Vault system is intended to store standardized data for reuse but does not currently format and validate data in-platform.

1. Log in via Globus & EMBER-Vault

  1. Log in to Globus using your institutional or any other authentication method you use to access the Globus Web UI
  2. Once you're logged in to Globus, navigate to your collections and ensure the default "Recent Tasks" filter is deactivated
  3. Search for "EMBER" and you should find your project's collection located on the Ember-Vault Endpoint
  4. Select your project's EMBER Vault collection by clicking on the name. In this case, it is EMBER-Vault YOUR-PROJECT-NAME
  5. This should take you to the collection manager. Here, you should select Open in File Manager as indicated in the figure below
  6. In the File Manager, you will be met with a warning that you are not authenticated with auth.emberarchive-vault.org. Press the Continue button in order to authenticate with EMBER-Vault

Note

If you have not yet created an account with EMBER-Vault and thus do not possess Keycloak credentials, please refer to the above section titled Account Setup

  1. You will then be redirected to EMBER-Vault's user login page. Here, you will sign in using your EMBER-Vault credentials which were generated during account setup. These should be a username provided to you by admins ending in @auth.emberarchive-vault.org and the password you set up. After this screen you will also be prompted to enter a one-time code from your MFA application

2. Select File/Folder to Upload

  1. Once you have signed in to Globus and EMBER-Vault, you can now access your EMBER-Vault project via the file manager. To begin uploading your data, click on the Upload button circled in the figure below.
  2. Clicking the Upload button will bring up an option to select files or a folder to upload to the collection from your local machine. For this demonstration, we will be uploading a folder
  3. You will be prompted to select a folder in your local system to upload to EMBER-Vault via Globus. Select your desired folder and click Upload
  4. You will then be prompted to confirm your upload, to do so select Upload
  5. You should then see in real time the upload progress of your file or each file in the folder you selected. Congratulations! You have successfully uploaded your data to EMBER-Vault :)

docs.title: Why do I need to standardize my data?
docs.text:
The ultimate goal for standardizing data is to enable secondary users to

  1. reproduce previous results (e.g., figures from papers) and
  2. reuse data for new analyses or models.

docs.title: Which standard should I use for my data?
docs.text:
EMBER accepts data packaged according to two standards: BIDS and NWB.

  • BIDS (Brain Imaging Data Specification) describes how to name files and organize them into appropriately named folders. It also requires metadata to describe data and the experiment.
  • NWB (Neurodata without Borders) is a single file that can hold multiple data streams and associated metadata that correspond to a single experimental session.

You can choose to convert your data into either standard, or a combination of both. The important considerations are:

  1. Quality and reusability — Does the standardized dataset contain enough information for someone unfamiliar with the experiment to understand and reuse it?
  2. Community Acceptance - What standard does your scientific community use, or what standards is your lab most familiar with?
  3. Fit to the existing data structure — Which standard requires the least unnecessary transformation from the original data representation?

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
You can use the following decision aid to help you decide whether your data should be converted into BIDS, NWB, or some hybrid. For more details, also refer to the Guidelines for BBQS Data Standards.

Data characteristic Standard My data are already separated by modality, session, and subject, and those modalities have established BIDS representations (e.g., separate EEG, video, audio, physiology, event, stimulus, or motion files). BIDS and BIDS extensions A single file (e.g., .mat, .h5) of my data contains multiple time series modalities within it and/or featurized data corresponding to the same recording session NWB and NWB extensions

If both descriptions apply to substantial portions of your dataset, consider a hybrid approach: use BIDS for the overall dataset organization and modalities that map naturally to established BIDS representations, and use NWB for integrated recordings that are better represented together.

For example, in the following dataset, the raw modalities (EEG and behavioral events) are represented in separate BIDS folders. In the BIDS derivatives folder, an NWB file that combines processed EEG, events, and kinematics represents the integrated data.

my_study/
├── dataset_description.json
├── participants.tsv
├── participants.json
│
├── sub-01/
│   └── ses-01/
│       ├── eeg/
│       │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_eeg.edf
│       │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_eeg.json
│       │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_channels.tsv
│       │   ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_electrodes.tsv
│       │   └── sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_events.tsv
│       │
│       └── beh/
│           ├── sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_beh.tsv
│           └── sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_beh.json
│
├── sub-02/
│   └── ses-01/
│       ├── eeg/
│       │   └── ...
│       └── beh/
│           └── ...
│
└── derivatives/
    └── integrated-nwb/
        ├── dataset_description.json
        │
        ├── sub-01/
        │   └── ses-01/
        │       └── sub-01_ses-01_task-walk_desc-integrated.nwb
        │
        └── sub-02/
            └── ses-01/
                └── sub-02_ses-01_task-walk_desc-integrated.nwb

docs.title: How to Standardize
docs.text:
To help you get started with writing conversions, we've published some of the prompts and conversion scripts we've put together for certain datasets at the BBQS data ingest repository.

For NWB specifically, you can also take a look at the Python library neuroconv, which converts data from proprietary formats to NWB.

docs.title: Quality Check
docs.text:
There are two quality checks:

  1. Is your standardized data correctly formatted with all necessary metadata? In other words, does this data pass the DANDI validator?
  2. Can your standardized data be used by a secondary analyst who has little to no knowledge of your data to, at a minimum, recreate figures from your paper?

The first check is relatively quick - once your data is standardized, you can run validation checks to ensure that it can be uploaded (see uploading data) without errors to EMBER.

The second (optional) check requires rebuilding analyses that were conducted on the original unstandardized data using the new, standardized data. At a minimum, this is recreation of figures generated for a publication. You can see an example of this from a BBQS team here.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text: If you need help or have any questions, please reach out to help@emberarchive.org.

docs.title: Uploading Data
docs.text:
These instructions will guide you on how to upload data to EMBER-DANDI.

Prerequisites

Please ensure that your data is formatted using NWB and BIDS before attempting to upload to EMBER-DANDI

My files are in a mix of standards or I have not used standards

Please contact the EMBER team at help@emberarchive.org to facilitate data ingestion into EMBER-DANDI. We are also happy to add you to our Slack workspace.

Below, we have provided one set of instructions for users that are new to EMBER-DANDI, and one set for experienced users. Please follow whichever best fits your needs:

  1. I've used DANDI or CLI tools before
  2. I'm new to Python, CLI, and/or DANDI
    • Learn how to set up Python, install the DANDI Client, and use NWB

docs.title: Instructions for Experienced Users
docs.text:
The following is a quick reference of the steps for uploading data using the DANDI Client: 

dandi download https://dandi.emberarchive.org/dandiset/<dandiset_id>/draft
cd <dandiset_id>
dandi organize <source_folder> -f dry
dandi organize <source_folder>
dandi validate .
dandi upload -i ember-dandi

docs.title: Install Python and the DANDI Client
docs.text: In these instructions, you will install Python 3.9+ and then install the DANDI Python Client.

docs.title: Install Python
docs.text:
If you're new to Python, it may be useful to start by checking out Python's Getting Started page There are many ways to install and use Python, so we've highlighted a few common ways to get started below.

  • Install Anaconda
  • Install uv

docs.title: Install the DANDI Client
docs.text:
Once you've gotten up and running with Python, the following command will install the DANDI Client: 

pip install -U dandi

docs.title: More Information
docs.text:
For more detailed information on the DANDI Python Client, please refer to the following resources:

  • DANDI Client on PyPI
  • DANDI Client docs

docs.title: Getting Started with NWB
docs.text:
For the latest information on NWB (Neurodata Without Borders), we recommend referring to their documentation at nwb.org!

Below, you will find a brief set of steps to help you quickly get started with NWB.

  1. We recommended installing the NWB Guide, a desktop application that converts common neuroscience data formats into NWB to enable uploading to EMBER-DANDI.
  2. Complete key tutorials for NWB GUIDE:
    • Generate a dataset
    • Convert a single session of data
    • Convert a multi-session of data
  3. Repeat steps with your own your data
    • Important Note: All data formats are not currently supported! Ensure your data is supported by checking the ecosystem compatibility

docs.title: Create an EMBER-DANDI dandiset
docs.text:
1. Log in to EMBER-DANDI with your approved GitHub account
  2. Select the "New Dandiset" button in the top right corner
  3. Fill out basic metadata and hit "Register Dandiset"
  4. Note that you can set your dataset to be private (embargoed) by selecting the toggle at the top. You'll be asked to set a date for the embargo to be released.

docs.title: Upload data to your dandiset
docs.text:
1. Validate your converted files, replacing <source_folder> with the path to your .nwb files: 

    dandi validate --ignore DANDI.NO_DANDISET_FOUND <source_folder>

  2. Navigate to your dandiset on EMBER-DANDI and copy the dandiset ID number

  1. Upload your validated .nwb files using the following commands, replacing <dandiset_id> and <source_folder> with your specific information: 

    dandi download https://dandi.emberarchive.org/dandiset/<dandiset_id>/draft
cd <dandiset_id>
dandi organize <source_folder> -f dry
dandi organize <source_folder>
dandi validate .
dandi upload -i ember-dandi
    4. You can publish your dataset at any point by either clicking "Publish" on a draft dandiset, or "Unembargo" and then "Publish".

Uploading Video Files

If using video files, replace dandi organize "source folder" with dandi organize --update-external-file-paths --files-mode copy /path/to/source_folder

Password Prompt

If this is your first upload, you may get a prompt to enter a password. In the EMBER-DANDI Portal, click on your user icon in the top right to retrieve your API key. Enter this when prompted for your password.
